name: Taffeta-Shoal
geological_features: Global shallow ocean with average depth of 50 meters
specific_features: Iridescent tidal flats that shimmer like taffeta when wet
Sea-grass meadows covering the shallow ocean floor
description: Taffeta-Shoal is a world of shallows. Its global ocean averages only fifty meters in depth, spread thin across the planet like water on a plate. Extensive tidal flats emerge twice daily as the planet's large moon pulls the shallow waters back and forth, exposing vast expanses of iridescent sediment that shimmer with metallic blues, greens, and purples like wet taffeta. The tidal range is enormous—up to twenty meters in some regions—creating a world that is constantly transforming between oceanic and terrestrial states, never fully one or the other.

The atmosphere is breathable and mild, carrying the constant salt-and-green scent of the sea-grass meadows that carpet the shallow ocean floor. These meadows are the planet's dominant life form, a photosynthetic organism that produces vast quantities of oxygen and serves as the foundation of an extensive food web. The sky is often hazy with sea spray lifted by gentle winds that circulate moisture from the ocean's enormous surface area. Weather is gentle—the shallow ocean cannot store enough heat to drive powerful storms, and the overall effect is of perpetual mild spring.

The tidal flats are the planet's most dynamic environment, ecosystems that must adapt to being submerged and exposed twice daily. The organisms that inhabit them are remarkable generalists, capable of photosynthesizing when exposed to air and switching to filter-feeding when submerged. The iridescent sediment is itself partly biological—the metallic sheen comes from mineral deposits laid down by microbial activity over millions of years, creating surfaces that function as both habitat and solar collector. The visual effect when the tide recedes is stunning, kilometers of shimmering fabric laid across the landscape.

Taffeta-Shoal's extreme shallowness makes it vulnerable to even modest geological changes. A rise in sea level of just a few meters would eliminate the tidal flats entirely, while a comparable drop would strand the sea-grass meadows above water. The planet exists in a narrow band of conditions that produces its unique character, and climate models suggest this balance has been maintained by biological feedback loops involving the sea-grass oxygen production and microbial mineral cycling. Disrupting these loops through colonization or resource extraction could push the system past a tipping point with unpredictable results. The shoal is resilient but delicate, a world balanced on the edge of its own tides.
